$comment: Historical airdrop research. Every numeric claim carries a source. A field that is not publicly sourced is null and stays null — it is never filled with an estimate. valueAtDistributionUsd and peakValueOfDistributedTokensUsd measure different things and are never interchanged.

methodology.rankingRule: Tokens actually distributed multiplied by a sourced distribution-day or TGE price, or a distribution-day value reported directly by a source. A case whose distribution-day valuation cannot be reconstructed from a source is marked rankingComparable: false and excluded from the ranking, though it keeps its article.
methodology.secondaryRule: The same distributed allocation valued at the token's all-time-high price. This is the peak value of the distributed allocation. It is never described as the value distributed at launch.
methodology.whyNotTheUsualList: The most-cited ranking of 'biggest airdrops' — CoinGecko's 50 Biggest Crypto Airdrops — values each distribution at the token's all-time high. On that basis Uniswap is first at $6.43B. Measured at what recipients actually received on distribution day, Uniswap's drop was worth about $450M and ranks seventh in this set. Both numbers are correct; they answer different questions.

basisLegend.reported: A publication stated the aggregate value directly.
basisLegend.computed: Tokens distributed multiplied by a sourced price.
basisLegend.derived: Back-calculated from another sourced figure; the derivation is stated on the case.
basisLegend.claimed: The token count is what recipients actually claimed.
basisLegend.allocated: The token count is what was set aside for the distribution; a separate claimed total is not sourced.

cases.antiSybilNote: Arkham did not publish a sybil-filtering methodology for this distribution.
cases.distributionMechanism: Claim-based. Eligible users connected a wallet and claimed ARKM from a distributor contract; tokens were not pushed to wallets.
cases.productBeforeToken: Arkham had been running an on-chain intelligence platform in private beta, plus a bounty marketplace paying users to deanonymise addresses, before ARKM existed.

whyItSucceeded.detail: Joining a waitlist and doing bounty work were both cheap, so the eligible population was wide rather than capital-gated.
The waitlist and bounty program existed to run the product, not to farm a future token, so the snapshot measured real platform interest.
ARKM launched through Binance Launchpad, so recipients had a deep venue on day one rather than a thin DEX pool.
Most recipients received under 200 ARKM and only five addresses received more than 100,000, so the drop spread across tens of thousands of wallets instead of concentrating.

weaknesses.detail: On-chain analysis found 95% of recipient wallets sold, and 80% liquidated their entire holding.
Because the eligible-wallet count was never published, the claim rate cannot be computed — and the on-chain recipient count gets misread as eligibility.

cases.postAirdropOutcome: ARKM traded actively from launch. Recipient behaviour skewed heavily toward selling: on-chain data showed 95% of the roughly 63,700 recipient wallets sold some ARKM and 80% sold their whole allocation.
cases.priceAfterNote: Dated 30-day and 90-day price marks are not published here because no primary source for them was verified.
lessons: A recipient count and an eligibility count are different measurements. 63,700 addresses received ARKM; that number says nothing about how many wallets qualified.
A claim-based airdrop has two different totals depending on when you read it — 47,000+ claimants on day one, roughly 63,700 recipients by the end of the window.
Where the eligible set is never disclosed, the claim rate is unknowable, and any 'X% claimed' figure is inferred rather than measured.
A signup-and-bounty funnel with no capital requirement still produced a distribution across tens of thousands of wallets.

cases.distributionMechanism: Claim-based against a published eligibility list, open for six months. Unclaimed ARB returned to the DAO treasury.
cases.productBeforeToken: Arbitrum One had been live for roughly eighteen months as the largest Ethereum rollup by total value locked before ARB existed.

whyItSucceeded.detail: Arbitrum was already the leading rollup by TVL, so the snapshot measured a real user base rather than an audience assembled to farm.
Points across bridging, duration, application diversity and value made a qualifying history expensive to manufacture.
625,143 eligible wallets was, at the time, one of the widest eligible sets ever published.
The eligible list and the criteria were both published before the claim opened, so the drop could be audited rather than trusted.

weaknesses.detail: The criteria rewarded behaviour that a determined farmer could have produced across many wallets over the qualifying period, and sybil filtering removed only the clusters it could detect.

eligibilityCriteria: Registered or held a .eth name at the 31 October 2021 snapshot.
Allocation scaled with how long the name had been held and how long it remained registered.
Setting a primary ENS name added a multiplier.
antiSybilRules: Registering a .eth name costs an annual fee plus gas, so each additional eligible wallet had a real recurring cost.
The duration multiplier meant a wallet registered shortly before the snapshot earned far less than a long-held name.
cases.distributionMechanism: Claim-based, open for roughly six months. Claimants had to delegate their voting power as part of the claim, and unclaimed ENS returned to the DAO treasury.
cases.productBeforeToken: ENS had run as Ethereum's naming system for four years, with names in active use as wallet addresses and profile identities, before the token existed.

whyItSucceeded.detail: A .eth name was already useful — it was how people received funds and identified themselves on-chain.
Annual registration fees made mass wallet farming expensive and the duration multiplier made recent registrations near-worthless.
The claim required delegating governance, so the drop bootstrapped a working DAO rather than a passive holder base.
The duration multiplier explicitly paid the people who had been there longest.

weaknesses.detail: 5.4M of 25M ENS went unclaimed — roughly a fifth of the allocation never reached a recipient.
The mandatory delegation step and Ethereum gas costs at the time deterred smaller allocations from claiming at all.

cases.postAirdropOutcome: ENS rose sharply after the claim opened. 103,000 of 137,689 eligible addresses claimed — a 75% claim rate, one of the few in this set that can actually be computed because both numbers were published.
cases.priceAfterNote: Dated 30-day and 90-day price marks are not published here because no primary source for them was verified.
lessons: This is the rare case where the claim rate is measurable, because the project published both the eligible count and the claimed count.
A recurring registration fee is a strong sybil filter: it makes every extra eligible wallet cost money every year.
Requiring delegation at claim time converts an airdrop into governance participation instead of pure distribution.

whyItSucceeded.detail: Because nobody knew a token was coming, nobody could farm the snapshot — the strongest sybil defence available, and one that can only be used once.

Uniswap was already the largest DEX; the snapshot measured a real user base.

A surprise retroactive drop is the only distribution design that is sybil-proof by construction, and it works exactly once per ecosystem.
A flat per-address allocation broadens ownership; a proportional one concentrates it. Uniswap did both, in separate tranches.

cases.productBeforeToken: Celestia had run public testnets and published its modular data-availability research for years, but the mainnet the token secured launched on the same day as the drop.

whyItSucceeded.detail: Nearly 585,000 eligible participants across three separate ecosystems.
A dedicated developer track paid open-source contributors, which almost no other major drop has done.
Eligibility spanned Ethereum rollups and Cosmos, seeding a user base in both communities at once.

weaknesses.detail: The mainnet launched with the token, so eligibility had to be borrowed from other chains' activity rather than measured on Celestia itself.

weaknesses.factor: Smallest distribution value in this set apart from Arkham
weaknesses.detail: At 6% of supply and a sub-$2 opening price, the drop's absolute value was an order of magnitude below the leaders.

cases.postAirdropOutcome: TIA opened near $1.90 and rose through the following months, peaking above $20 in early 2024.
cases.priceAfterNote: Dated 30-day and 90-day price marks are not published here because no primary source for them was verified.
lessons: A chain with no history has to borrow its eligibility signal from other ecosystems, which measures adjacency rather than usage.
Paying open-source contributors is a distinct eligibility track and one of the few that cannot be farmed with wallets.

eligibilityCriteria: Used Starknet above a transaction and value threshold before the snapshot.
Staked ETH on the Ethereum beacon chain.
Contributed to eligible Ethereum or Starknet open-source repositories.

antiSybilRules: Ethereum staking eligibility required 32 ETH per validator, which is capital-gated by construction.
Developer eligibility was assessed on identifiable repository contribution history.
cases.distributionMechanism: Claim-based, open for four months, across five separate eligibility tracks.
cases.productBeforeToken: Starknet had run as a live Ethereum validity rollup for over two years, and StarkEx had powered dYdX v3 and Immutable X for longer, before STRK existed.

whyItSucceeded.detail: Nearly 1.3 million eligible addresses — the widest eligible set in this research set.
Ethereum open-source contributors were an explicit eligibility track alongside on-chain users.
Ethereum stakers and StarkEx application users were eligible even if they had never touched Starknet.

weaknesses.detail: The distribution drew sustained community criticism over which groups were and were not included, and a subsequent fix largely targeted validators.
The launch-day price range is wide enough and the reporting inconsistent enough that this case cannot be ranked on distribution value at all.

cases.postAirdropOutcome: STRK traded down substantially from its launch-day highs over the following months, and the allocation rules remained contested within the community.
cases.priceAfterNote: Dated 30-day and 90-day price marks are not published here because no primary source for them was verified.
lessons: When a token's all-time high prints on its distribution day, the two measurements this research keeps apart collapse into one — and the honest response is to publish neither rather than to pick the flattering one.
Breadth is not the same as acceptance: the widest eligible set in this set also produced the loudest disputes about who was left out.
